lesson.text: Quick memory: in grade 3, what makes a sculpture good to walk around? (It looks good from every side.) Today: big 3D works, and installations that fill a whole space.
Sculpture can be carved, modelled, cast or built. Barbara Hepworth (1903-1975) and Henry Moore (1898-1986) carved and cast smooth forms with holes that let light and air through.
An installation is art you step into. It fills a room or a place, and the visitor becomes part of it. Light, sound and the way people move can all be part of the work.
Big works can fill a park. Louise Bourgeois (1911-2010) made Maman (1999), a spider over 9 m tall. In 2005 Christo and Jeanne-Claude set 7,503 orange gates along the paths of a New York park.
Alexander Calder (1898-1976) made the first mobiles in the 1930s: shapes hanging from arms that turn in the air. An arm balances when weight × distance is the same on both sides.
Worked example: 3 units of weight 2 steps out balance 2 units 3 steps out, as 3 × 2 = 6 and 2 × 3 = 6. Move a shape further out and its side turns down.
Plan a big work with a maquette, a small model to scale. At 1:20, every 1 cm of model is 20 cm of the real work. Think about safety, light, weather and how visitors move round it.
Try it in the world: make a small mobile from a coat hanger, string and card shapes, and balance it. In LIFE, Real Builder lets you build at real size, brick by brick. Next: your exhibition.

exercises.prompt: What makes an installation different from a painting?
choices: you step into it and are part of it
it is only made of paint
exercises.hint: Where are you when you see an installation?
exercises.explain: An installation fills a space you walk into, so you become part of the work.

exercises.prompt: A mobile's arm balances when weight × distance is the same on both sides.
exercises.explain: True: equal weight × distance on each side means neither side turns down.

exercises.prompt: The mobile balances. What is the hidden weight?
exercises.hint: Work out the known side's weight × distance first.
exercises.explain: Left: 3 × 2 = 6. Right: ? × 3 = 6, so the hidden weight is 6 ÷ 3 = 2.

exercises.prompt: Match each way of making sculpture to what it means.
exercises.hint: Think of taking away, adding, pouring and joining.
exercises.explain: Carving takes away, modelling builds up, casting pours into a mould and assembling joins parts.

exercises.prompt: This arm is held still. Which way will it tip when it is let go?
exercises.hint: Work out weight × distance on each side.
exercises.explain: Left: 4 × 3 = 12. Right: 2 × 2 = 4. The left turns more, so the left side goes down.

exercises.prompt: The mobile balances. What is the hidden weight?
exercises.hint: Add up the left side's turning first.
exercises.explain: Left: 4 × 1 + 2 × 4 = 12. Right: ? × 2 = 12, so the hidden weight is 6.

exercises.prompt: A maquette is made at 1:20. It is 15 cm tall. How tall is the real sculpture, in cm?
exercises.hint: At 1:20 the real work is 20 times the model.

exercises.prompt: An installation, or a sculpture on a stand?
items: a room of mirrors you walk through
a bronze head on a stand
lights and sounds filling a hall
exercises.hint: Do you step into it, or look at it from outside?
exercises.explain: Mirror rooms, lights filling a hall and gates along paths surround you; a bronze head and a stone bird stand alone to be looked at.

exercises.prompt: Maman by Louise Bourgeois is a spider over 9 m tall.
exercises.explain: True: Maman, of 1999, stands over 9 m tall.

exercises.prompt: Order the steps of planning an installation.
items: check safety and how people move
exercises.hint: Know the space first; build big last.
exercises.explain: Measure, sketch, make a maquette, check safety and movement, then build it full size.

exercises.prompt: Why do sculptors make a maquette first?
choices: to test the idea small before building big
because it is the finished work
exercises.hint: Is it cheaper to change a small model or a huge work?
exercises.explain: A small model shows problems early, when they are cheap and easy to fix.

exercises.prompt: The mobile balances. What is the hidden weight?
exercises.hint: Add up the right side's turning first.
exercises.explain: Right: 6 × 2 + 1 × 4 = 16. Left: ? × 4 = 16, so the hidden weight is 16 ÷ 4 = 4.

exercises.prompt: A sculpture will be 4 m tall. How tall is its maquette at 1:20, in cm?
exercises.hint: Turn metres into centimetres, then divide by 20.

exercises.prompt: This arm is held still. Which way will it tip when it is let go?
exercises.hint: Compare weight × distance; the heavier shape is not always the winner.
exercises.explain: Left: 2 × 5 = 10. Right: 3 × 3 = 9. The lighter shape is further out, so the left turns down.

exercises.prompt: Moving a shape further from the middle makes its side turn down more.
exercises.explain: True: a bigger distance makes weight × distance bigger, so that side turns more.

exercises.prompt: Safe for visitors, or a risk?
items: a dark floor with a hidden step
exercises.hint: Imagine walking through it with a younger child.
exercises.explain: Fixed parts, clear exits and steady lights keep visitors safe; sharp edges and hidden steps are risks.
